positions/contemplative-revival/name: The modern contemplative revival (Merton, Centering Prayer)
positions/contemplative-revival/oneLine: The ancient contemplative tradition of silent, loving attention to God should be recovered for all Christians today, through simple practices like Centering Prayer or the Christian mantra, often in dialogue with other religious traditions.
positions/contemplative-revival/coreClai: Contemplation is the birthright of all the baptised, not only monks.
Silent prayer of consent to God’s presence heals the false self.
The Cloud of Unknowing, the Desert Fathers and Carmelites provide the method.
Dialogue with Eastern meditation can help Christians rediscover their own tradition.
positions/contemplative-revival/origin: Popularised by Thomas Merton from 1948; Centering Prayer developed by Trappists William Meninger, Basil Pennington and Thomas Keating at Spencer, Massachusetts (c.1975); Christian Meditation taught by Benedictine John Main (1975); spread among Protestants through Richard Foster’s Celebration of Discipline (1978) and the Renovaré movement.
positions/contemplative-revival/stronges: It restores neglected treasures of the Christian tradition.
It meets a modern hunger for silence and depth.
It offers an ecumenical common practice.
Evangelical critics argue it imports Eastern techniques and seeks an experience of God not mediated by Scripture.
The Catholic Congregation for the Doctrine of the Faith (1989) warned against uncritical adoption of non-Christian methods.
Some see its claims about the "true self" as psychology dressed in theology.
positions/contemplative-revival/response: Practitioners root it in Christian sources and insist it is prayer to the triune God, complementary to Scripture and sacraments.
positions/contemplative-revival/conseque: Retreat centres, spiritual direction programmes and contemplative networks.
positions/celtic-spirituality/altNames/0: Early Irish and British monastic spirituality
positions/celtic-spirituality/oneLine: Early Irish, Scottish and Welsh Christianity offers a spirituality of God’s presence in creation and daily work, of blessing prayers for every task, of pilgrimage and of vigorous ascetic monastic mission.
positions/celtic-spirituality/coreClaims: God and the saints are present in landscape, home and work.
Prayers and blessings sanctify ordinary tasks (kindling the fire, milking, travelling).
Pilgrimage ("white martyrdom") and penitential asceticism are paths to God.
Monastic communities (Iona, Lindisfarne) are centres of prayer and mission.
positions/celtic-spirituality/keyTexts/2: Lorica of St Patrick ("St Patrick’s Breastplate", traditionally attributed)
positions/celtic-spirituality/origin: Rooted in the monastic churches founded by Patrick (5th c.), Columba (Iona, 563) and Aidan (Lindisfarne, 635); revived in the 19th-20th centuries through Carmina Gadelica and movements such as the Iona Community (1938) and Northumbria Community.
positions/celtic-spirituality/strongestA: It affirms the goodness of creation and the sanctity of daily life.
Its prayers are rich, poetic and accessible.
Its monks were remarkable missionaries across Europe.
positions/celtic-spirituality/strongestO: Historians (e.g. Ian Bradley) show that much modern "Celtic spirituality" is romantic invention, projecting modern ecological or anti-institutional ideals onto the past.
The real early Irish church was also severely ascetic and fully part of Latin Christendom.
positions/celtic-spirituality/responses/: Advocates accept the historical corrections while valuing the prayers and the vision for today.
positions/celtic-spirituality/consequenc: Iona and Northumbria communities; Celtic-style liturgies.
positions/philokalic-revival/name: The Philokalia and the Orthodox elders
positions/philokalic-revival/oneLine: The hesychast heritage, gathered in the Philokalia (1782), is for every Christian: unceasing prayer of the heart, guided by a spiritual elder (geron, starets), leads to the acquisition of the Holy Spirit.
positions/philokalic-revival/coreClaims/: Watchfulness and the Jesus Prayer are for laity as well as monks.
Spiritual fathers and mothers (elders) guide discernment.
The aim of the Christian life is acquiring the Holy Spirit (Seraphim of Sarov).
Frequent communion and prayer unite the believer to Christ.
positions/philokalic-revival/origin: Compiled by Nicodemus the Hagiorite and Macarius of Corinth (Venice, 1782); translated into Slavonic by Paisius Velichkovsky (1793), feeding the 19th-century elders of Optina and Seraphim of Sarov, and the Way of a Pilgrim; renewed in Romania (Stăniloae) and on Athos in the 20th century.
positions/philokalic-revival/strongestAr: It made patristic spirituality available to ordinary believers.
Elders offered personal, compassionate guidance in times of upheaval.
It sustained Orthodox faith under Ottoman and Soviet rule.
positions/philokalic-revival/strongestOb: Some Orthodox bishops historically distrusted charismatic elders operating outside hierarchical control.
Critics warn of unhealthy dependence on elders ("elder-ism").
Western critics raise the same questions as for hesychasm.
positions/philokalic-revival/responses/0: The tradition itself stresses obedience to the Church and warns against false elders.
positions/philokalic-revival/consequence: Optina Hermitage and Russian eldership; global interest in the Jesus Prayer.
positions/dawn-prayer-movements/name: Korean dawn prayer and African prayer movements
positions/dawn-prayer-movements/oneLine: Daily corporate prayer before dawn, loud simultaneous prayer (tongsong kido), fasting on prayer mountains and all-night vigils express dependence on God and fuel revival and church growth.
positions/dawn-prayer-movements/coreClai: Seek God early and corporately every day (Psalm 5:3; Mark 1:35).
Everyone prays aloud together, pouring out the heart.
Fasting and retreats to prayer mountains intensify prayer.
Prayer brings healing, protection and revival in situations of suffering.
positions/dawn-prayer-movements/origin: Korean daily dawn prayer is traditionally traced to elder Gil Seon-ju at Jangdaehyeon Church, Pyongyang (1906), and the Great Revival of 1907; prayer mountains spread from the 1940s-70s (e.g. Osanri, Yoido Full Gospel Church). In West Africa the Aladura churches (from 1918-30) and in East Africa the Revival (from 1930s) made intense prayer central.
positions/dawn-prayer-movements/proponen: Redeemed Christian Church of God Holy Ghost Congress
positions/dawn-prayer-movements/stronges: It shows a deep, communal dependence on God that Western churches admire.
It is linked to remarkable church growth and resilience under persecution.
Critics warn that prayer can become a means of securing prosperity or success.
Some see pressure, exhaustion or competition in prayer cultures.
Outsiders sometimes mistake cultural intensity for spiritual depth or vice versa.
positions/dawn-prayer-movements/response: Participants testify that dawn prayer forms discipline and humility, and leaders warn against prosperity distortions.
positions/dawn-prayer-movements/conseque: Korean megachurches and missions; African prayer camps and vigils.
Global prayer movements influenced by Korean practice.
positions/word-centred-piety/oneLine: God meets us not by climbing ladders of ascent or by wordless union but by coming down to us in his Word and sacraments; prayer is the response of faith to God’s promises in Scripture, offered through Christ alone.
positions/word-centred-piety/coreClaims/: Faith comes by hearing the Word (Romans 10:17); the Spirit works through the Word.
Prayer is answering God’s promises, not achieving union by technique.
Christ is the only mediator; there is no ladder of merit or ascent.
Ordinary vocation and the Lord’s Prayer are the school of prayer.
positions/word-centred-piety/keyTexts/4: Luther, A Simple Way to Pray (1535)
positions/word-centred-piety/origin: Formed in Luther’s critique of "enthusiasts" and of Dionysian mystical ascent (from 1520), Calvin’s teaching on prayer, and later in 20th-century theology: Barth and Emil Brunner’s polemic (Die Mystik und das Wort, 1924) contrasting mysticism and the Word.
positions/word-centred-piety/strongestAr: It keeps prayer tied to God’s revealed Word and to Christ.
It guards against spiritual elitism and technique.
It makes prayer accessible to every believer in ordinary life.
positions/word-centred-piety/strongestOb: Mystics reply that Scripture itself speaks of union, vision and contemplation (2 Corinthians 3:18; 2 Peter 1:4).
Critics say it can become arid and intellectualist.
Luther himself valued Tauler and the Theologia Germanica, so the opposition is overdrawn.
positions/word-centred-piety/responses/0: Many Protestants now combine Word-centred prayer with practices like lectio divina and silence, arguing these are ways of attending to the Word.
positions/contemplative-prayer-critique/: Critiques of contemplative prayer techniques
Evangelical critique of contemplative spirituality
CDF cautions (1989)

Christian prayer is personal dialogue with the triune God through Christ, grounded in Scripture; methods that empty the mind, repeat words mechanically or seek altered states risk importing non-Christian spirituality.
Jesus warns against "vain repetitions" (Matthew 6:7).
Biblical meditation is filling the mind with God’s Word, not emptying it.
Experiences must be tested by Scripture; feelings of union are not self-authenticating.
Borrowing from Hindu or Buddhist techniques may confuse the Creator-creature distinction.
Matthew 6:7-9
Psalm 1:2
Philippians 4:8
1 John 4:1
CDF, Orationis formas (1989)

Voiced by Catholic authorities (the Congregation for the Doctrine of the Faith’s 1989 letter on Christian meditation) and especially by evangelical and Reformed writers since the 1980s-90s responding to Centering Prayer, Transcendental Meditation and the spread of "spiritual formation" in evangelical churches.
Joseph Ratzinger (as CDF prefect)
Evangelical apologetics writers
Reformed critics of the spiritual formation movement
It protects the distinctiveness of Christian prayer.
It insists on Scripture as the test of experience.
It warns against spiritual consumerism and technique.
Contemplatives reply that the methods come from Christian sources (Cassian, the Cloud, the Jesus Prayer), not from the East.
Critics say it caricatures contemplative practice and overlooks biblical silence (Psalm 46:10; 1 Kings 19:12).
Critics distinguish acceptable silence and meditation on Scripture from mind-emptying techniques; the CDF letter itself affirms Christian contemplation while warning against confusion.
Debates within evangelical seminaries and churches about spiritual formation.
positions/protestant-vocation-asceticism: Asceticism debated: monastic vows versus vocation in the world
Worldly asceticism
Priesthood of all believers
Critique of monastic vows

Holiness is not a higher grade reached by vows of poverty, chastity and obedience but the calling of every Christian in marriage, work and household; true asceticism is daily self-denial in ordinary vocation.
All baptised Christians are priests and have holy callings (1 Peter 2:9).
Vows not commanded by God cannot earn merit; marriage and work are honourable callings.
Self-denial and discipline belong to everyday life ("inner-worldly asceticism", in Weber’s phrase).
1 Peter 2:9
1 Corinthians 7:17-24
Colossians 2:20-23
1 Timothy 4:1-5
Luther, On Monastic Vows (1521)

Articulated by Luther in On Monastic Vows (1521) and by other Reformers, leading to the dissolution of monasteries in Protestant lands (e.g. England 1536-40). Catholic and Orthodox traditions defended monastic life as a gift and sign of the Kingdom; Anglican and Lutheran religious communities later revived it.
Max Weber (sociological interpreter)
Anglican Oxford Movement (revival of religious orders)
Taizé (Protestant monastic community, 1940s)
It honours ordinary life and work as service to God.
It rejects two-tier Christianity.
It corrected real abuses in late-medieval monasteries.
Catholic and Orthodox critics answer that Jesus and Paul commend celibacy and renunciation for some (Matthew 19:12, 21; 1 Corinthians 7:7-8).
The loss of monasteries removed centres of prayer, learning and care for the poor.
Protestant revivals of community life suggest something was lost.
Reformers did not reject discipline or celibacy as such but compulsory vows and merit; later Protestant communities (Taizé, Anglican orders) seek a balance.
Dissolution of the monasteries; the Protestant work ethic debate.
Revival of religious communities among Anglicans and Lutherans.
